Delicate
dĕl´ĭ-kāt
adj. (softly reared; pampered; unaccustomed to hardship; Hebrew 'anog, rak)
Latin delicatus, giving pleasure, luxurious. In the KJV it never means fragile by nature; it means softened by ease, and it is normally the prelude to a judgment.

Biblical Definition

Scripture's delicate man or woman is not frail by constitution but softened by comfort, and the word almost always stands in a siege or a captivity. Moses warns of what famine will do to the gentlest among them: “So that the man that is tender among you, and very delicate, his eye shall be evil toward his brother, and toward the wife of his bosom” (Deu 28:54), and the companion verse is worse: “The tender and delicate woman among you, which would not adventure to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness, her eye shall be evil toward the husband of her bosom” (Deu 28:56). Isaiah says it to Babylon: “Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate” (Isa 47:1). Jeremiah says it to Judah: “I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate woman” (Jer 6:2), and an army is at the gate by the next verse. Micah mourns the children of it: “Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children… for they are gone into captivity from thee” (Mic 1:16). Ease is not neutral. Deuteronomy 28 says it does not survive contact with hunger.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines delicate as pleasing to the senses; nice; soft; effeminate; and, of persons, tender, unable to endure hardship.

expand to see more

DELICATE, a. Of an agreeable flavor; pleasing to the taste; as a delicate viand.

2. Nice; pleasing to the senses; fine.

3. Soft; effeminate; not able to endure hardship; as a delicate person.

4. Requiring nice handling; as a delicate question.

Key Scripture

Deu 28:54 — "So that the man that is tender among you, and very delicate, his eye shall be evil toward his brother, and toward the wife of his bosom, and toward the remnant of his children which he shall leave:"

Deu 28:56 — "The tender and delicate woman among you, which would not adventure to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness, her eye shall be evil toward the husband of her bosom, and toward her son, and toward her daughter,"

Isa 47:1 — "Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate."

Jer 6:2 — "I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate woman."

Modern Corruption

Comfort is treated as a neutral condition, while Deuteronomy makes softness the thing that fails first and worst under pressure.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 28:54–56 is unbearable to read and impossible to misunderstand. The tender and delicate woman who would not set the sole of her foot upon the ground is the one whose eye becomes evil toward her own children in the siege. Moses is not saying that gentle people are secretly cruel. He is saying that a soul kept from every hardship has no reserves, and that when the hardship comes anyway it discovers what was never built. This is the plainest biblical argument against raising children, or churches, on comfort.

The therapeutic instinct of the present age is to treat every discomfort as an injury to be prevented, and it produces exactly the person Deuteronomy describes. Scripture's alternative is not harshness but training — no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness. Hebrews assumes hardship is coming and asks what it will find; Deuteronomy shows what it finds in the delicate.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'anog (H6028), dainty, delicate, softened by luxury; rak (H7390), tender, soft; 'anugah, the delicateness of Deuteronomy 28:56.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'anog (H6028) — delicate, dainty; Deuteronomy 28:54, 28:56, Isaiah 47:1.

Hebrew rak (H7390) — tender, soft; paired with delicate in every warning.

Hebrew 'anugah (H6026) — delicateness; the state, not the temperament.

Hebrew ta'anug (H8588) — luxury, exquisite delight; Micah 1:16, the delicate children.

Hebrew bath-tsiyon — daughter of Zion; likened to a comely and delicate woman, Jeremiah 6:2.

Usage

"“The tender and delicate woman among you” — and the siege is the subject."

"“Thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate” — said to Babylon on the ground."

"“Poll thee for thy delicate children” — ease does not travel into captivity."
